title: Fees: modes, caps, agreements and collection
objectives: Compare the two fee modes and compute a fee.
State the agreement, advance-fee and refund rules.
body_md:
## Two fee modes

| Mode | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Assets under advice (AUA)** | Fee as a % of the assets the adviser advises on, up to a **cap of 2.5% a year** per client |
| **Fixed fee** | A flat amount, capped at about **₹1,51,000 a year per family** for individual and HUF clients |

The caps apply to individual and HUF clients; accredited investors and non-individuals have different treatment. **Verify the current cap before quoting it.**

## Rules around the fee

- A **written agreement** fixes the services, the fee, the mode and the termination terms.
- Fees are collected through **banking channels**, and no more than **one quarter in advance**.
- On early exit, refund the unused portion on a pro-rata basis.
- Fees must be **reasonable and disclosed**; no commission, rebate or kickback from products.
- The adviser cannot take fees in a way that depends on the performance unless the rules allow it (they generally do not for IAs).

## Worked fee

Client advised on ₹40 lakh at 1.5% AUA: ₹60,000 a year, collected as ₹15,000 a quarter.

## Compare modes

Fixed fee suits clients with large assets; AUA suits small and growing portfolios, but check the cap does not exceed the client's benefit.

> **Exam tip:** Advance fee: at most one quarter. Fee-only: no product commission.
example: AUA ₹40 lakh at 1.5% gives ₹60,000 a year. The client pays ₹15,000 each quarter and may leave with a pro-rata refund.
say: My fee is fixed in a written agreement and I take no commission.
If you leave early, the unused fee is refunded.
never: I will take a year's fee in advance.
The fee depends on how much you gain.

check.q: An investment adviser may collect fees in advance for at most:
check.why: At most one quarter in advance.
